rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient that spans almost the full solvent range, so all 10 compounds are likely to elute without truncation and we can map the retention window and crowding pattern. A 20 min gradient is a balanced first probe that should reveal whether the mixture is broadly distributed or tightly clustered.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only available gain is reducing t_last by steepening the gradient while keeping the same wide composition window and temperature. A moderate step from 20 to 16 min should test how much time can be shaved before the closest mid-run pairs begin to approach the 1.5 resolution threshold.

The 16 min method is nearly ideal and the limiting pair is just above the 1.5 threshold, so the next step is a small further reduction in gradient time to see if we can bring t_last to 10 min or less without sacrificing full resolution. Dropping to 14 min is the most direct exploitation move before changing window or temperature.

The optimum is near the 16 min condition, but the limiting pair lost too much resolution at 14 min; raising temperature may recover speed and can alter selectivity enough to improve that critical pair while keeping t_last near or below 10 min. Testing 16 min at 45 C probes whether temperature can outperform the current best without sacrificing full resolution.

Higher temperature worsened the critical 6/7 pair badly, so test the opposite direction: a lower temperature may improve selectivity for that pair while preserving the favorable 16 min timing. This checks whether we can keep full resolution and perhaps still bring the last peak to about 10 min by thermal tuning.

Temperature tuning hurt selectivity, so keep the favorable 40 C and 16 min but narrow the gradient window slightly from the weak end to compress the early space and effectively shallow the gradient across the crowded middle. Raising phi0 to 0.10 may improve the critical mid-run separation while also nudging late elution a bit earlier.

The adjusted window at phi0 0.10 restored full resolution and brought t_last very close to 10 min, so the next logical move is a small cut in gradient time to try to eliminate the remaining time penalty. This tests whether the improved selectivity margin is enough to keep the critical pair above 1.5 at a faster run.

At 14 min the critical pair falls below threshold, so keep tG at 16 and continue narrowing the gradient from the weak end to further improve the crowded middle while shaving a little more retention from the tail. Increasing phi0 to 0.15 is a conservative one-step refinement around the current best method.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so the only remaining objective is to find the shortest fully resolved method. Reducing tG from 16 to 14 min at the current optimal window directly tests whether we can keep all pairs at or above 1.5 while shortening the run further.

Since 14 min is too fast at phi0 0.15, keep tG at 16 and raise phi0 one more step to see if the crowded mid-region gains enough selectivity margin to allow an even shorter method afterward. This also checks whether a narrower effective gradient can preserve full resolution while keeping the last peak comfortably under 10 min.

The best method is already fully resolved, so now probe whether trimming the strong-end limit can shorten the tail while maintaining the favorable selectivity around the critical 6/7 pair. Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 keeps the same 0.75 gradient span as the 0.20–0.95 test but preserves the successful 0.15 starting composition.

The 0.15–0.90 window improved the critical pair margin versus 0.15–0.95 at the same 16 min, suggesting it may better tolerate a shorter gradient. Testing 14 min here is the best chance to find a shorter fully resolved method than the current 16 min optimum.

The 0.15–0.90 window gives extra resolution margin, so a temperature increase is worth retesting there to see whether the last peak can be pulled under 10 min while keeping the critical pair above 1.5. This is a focused attempt to match the 1.000 score with a shorter thermal-accelerated run than the current best.

Higher temperature again collapses the critical pair, so stay at 40 C and continue exploring the composition window instead. Lowering phi1 to 0.85 with phi0 fixed at 0.15 may further improve selectivity around the 6/7 pair and could still keep the last peak under 10 min, giving another route to a 1.000 method.

The 0.15–0.85 window gives the largest resolution margin yet for the critical pair, so it is the best candidate to support a shorter gradient. Reducing to 14 min tests whether that extra margin is enough to retain full resolution while pulling the last peak back under 10 min.

We now have a second 1.000 method, so the next step is to keep shortening from this successful window until resolution drops below the threshold. Testing 12 min directly determines whether an even faster fully resolved method exists in the same selectivity region.

At 12 min with phi1 0.85 the critical pair is under-resolved, so slightly widening the strong-end limit to 0.90 may recover enough separation while still keeping the faster 12 min run. This is the most targeted way to see whether a 12 min fully resolved method is achievable near the successful 0.15 window.

Both 0.85 and 0.95 at 14 min bracket the resolution threshold, with 0.85 and 0.95 each just acceptable and 0.90 intermediate but still below full credit at shorter tG; pushing phi1 one step lower to 0.80 at 14 min tests whether extra selectivity can preserve full resolution while potentially defining the shortest robust window. This is a targeted boundary check around the current 14 min optimum family.

The 0.15–0.80 window gives the strongest resolution margin for the critical pair at 14 min, so it is the best remaining candidate to support a 12 min fully resolved method. This tests whether the added selectivity can offset the faster gradient and beat the current shortest 1.000 methods.

At 12 min the 0.15–0.80 window is closest yet to full resolution, and lower temperature previously shifted selectivity in the crowded region enough to change the limiting pair. Dropping to 35 C is a focused attempt to recover the remaining resolution margin for the 6/7 region while staying at the faster 12 min gradient.

Lower temperature did not help, so return to 40 C and try lowering phi0 one step while keeping the promising 0.80 upper limit and 12 min gradient. This slightly broadens the window and may restore enough separation in the crowded middle to push the critical pair above 1.5 at the faster method.

All 12 min attempts remain just below the resolution threshold, so use the remaining runs to search for the shortest robust 14 min variant. Testing phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.85 explores a narrower window than the successful 0.15–0.85 method and may retain full resolution with a shorter overall run profile.

The 0.20–0.85 window at 14 min was still slightly under-resolved, so increase phi1 one step to 0.90 to see if that restores the critical pair while keeping the same short 14 min program. This is a targeted final refinement around the faster high-phi0 region.

The search indicates the optimum lies on a narrow ridge around 14 min and moderate phi0/phi1, so test the complementary corner not yet explored: lower phi0 with phi1 0.85 at 14 min. This may reveal a slightly more favorable balance for the critical pair than the 0.15 or 0.20 starts while still staying in the shortest viable gradient range.

With one run left, the best use is a final shortest-method test adjacent to the newly found 14 min fully resolved condition, which has slightly better margin than the earlier 12 min trials. Dropping tG to 12 min here directly checks whether this window can deliver the fastest acceptable method, while the existing 1.000 methods are already secured if it fails.
